correctness.rationale: An order-n de Bruijn cycle is an Euler circuit of the directed de Bruijn graph with vertices length n-1 and arcs length n. Prescribing an (n+1)-word is equivalent to demanding two specified arcs e and f be consecutive. Identical arcs arise exactly for constants and are impossible. For distinct arcs contracting the two-arc path to a shortcut gives a balanced directed graph; such a graph is Eulerian iff its nonisolated support is weakly connected. Deleting any middle vertex leaves the other vertices connected because a lower-order de Bruijn Hamilton cycle supplies a spanning path after deletion. Only the middle vertex can be separated by removing e,f: nonconstant vertices retain nonloop incident arcs for q≥2; constant vertices retain the loop and q-2 other incident edges unless q=2, when choosing the two unique nonloop entering and exiting arcs isolates them. This yields precisely ba^(n-1)b with a≠b in binary. Independently enumerated all candidate shortcut circuits at (q,n)=(2,2),(2,3),(2,4),(3,2),(3,3),(4,2), matching the exact forbidden sets. These finite checks do not replace the Eulerian all-q,n proof.
